plan.chapterName: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, chapter 8: Advanced Theories of Covalent Bonding
plan.contextChunk: This figure sets three block diagrams side by side, each a schematic picture of the molecular orbital bands of a solid with energy increasing upward. Every diagram is built the same way: a lower blue-violet rectangle labeled Valence, an upper green rectangle labeled Conduction, and between them an empty white region whose left and right edges are marked by vertical dashed lines and which is spanned by a double-headed vertical arrow labeled Band gap. The leftmost diagram, headed Insulator, is drawn with the widest separation, its conduction block sitting far above the valence block. The middle diagram, headed Semiconductor, repeats the construction with a gap roughly half as tall, and the whole stack sits lower on the page. The rightmost diagram, headed Conductor, shows the two blocks almost touching, the gap reduced to a thin white sliver so narrow that its Band gap label has to be placed outside the diagram to the right. Since the three diagrams share identical block widths and colors, the only quantity that changes across the row is the height of the white region, which is what the reader is meant to measure by eye. The progression underlies the account of electrical conduction in solids, in which electrons must be promoted out of the filled valence band into the empty conduction band and the energy needed to do so is set by the separation between them.

interactionPlan.concept: Whether a solid conducts electricity depends on the size of the band gap between its filled valence band and empty conduction band — the smaller the gap, the easier it is to promote electrons and the better it conducts.

demo_steps.title: Compare the three panels
demo_steps.narration: All three diagrams are built identically — valence band below, conduction band above. The only thing that changes is the height of the white band gap: largest for the insulator, half as big for the semiconductor, nearly zero for the conductor.

demo_steps.title: Try to promote an electron
demo_steps.narration: Click each panel to attempt an electron promotion. In the conductor the electron crosses almost effortlessly; in the insulator the arrow falls far short — the gap is the energy barrier an electron must overcome.

demo_steps.title: Sweep the gap
demo_steps.narration: Drag the slider to shrink and grow the gap and watch the material's label switch between conductor, semiconductor, and insulator — the categories are points on one continuous scale of band-gap energy.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Electrical conduction in a solid is governed by a single number — the band gap energy — because an electron can only carry current after being promoted across that gap from the filled valence band into the conduction band.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Three side-by-side panels sharing identical block widths and colors: blue-violet 'Valence' block at bottom, green 'Conduction' block above, white gap between them edged with vertical dashed lines. Insulator (left) has the tallest gap with a double-headed arrow and 'Band gap' label inside; Semiconductor (middle) has roughly half that gap, same arrow construction, and its whole stack sits slightly lower; Conductor (right) has only a thin white sliver, with its 'Band gap' label placed outside to the right. Panel titles in bold above each. For the interactive version, one panel can be driven by the slider while the three canonical examples remain as reference; on click, animate an electron (small dot with upward arrow) from the valence block — it lands in the conduction band when the gap is small and stalls/falls back when the gap is large, with a proportional energy marker beside it.

authoredContext:
In a solid, similar things happen, but on a much larger scale. Remember that even in a small sample there are a huge number of atoms (typically > 1023 atoms), and therefore a huge number of atomic orbitals that may be combined into molecular orbitals. When N valence atomic orbitals, all of the same energy and each containing one (1) electron, are combined, N/2 (filled) bonding orbitals and N/2 (empty) antibonding orbitals will result. Each bonding orbital will show an energy lowering as the atomic orbitals are mostly in-phase, but each of the bonding orbitals will be a little different and have slightly different energies. The antibonding orbitals will show an increase in energy as the atomic orbitals are mostly out-of-phase, but each of the antibonding orbitals will also be a little different and have slightly different energies. The allowed energy levels for all the bonding orbitals are so close together that they form a band, called the valence band. Likewise, all the antibonding orbitals are very close together and form a band, called the conduction band. The figure shows the bands for three important classes of materials: insulators, semiconductors, and conductors.

Molecular orbitals in solids are so closely spaced that they are described as bands. The valence band is lower in energy and the conduction band is higher in energy. The type of solid is determined by the size of the “band gap” between the valence and conduction bands. Only a very small amount of energy is required to move electrons from the valence band to the conduction band in a conductor, and so they conduct electricity well. In an insulator, the band gap is large, so that very few electrons move, and they are poor conductors of electricity. Semiconductors are in between: they conduct electricity better than insulators, but not as well as conductors.

This figure shows three diagrams. The first is labeled, “Insulator,” and it consists of two boxes. The “conduction” box is above and the “valence” box is below. A large gap marked by 4 dashed lines contains a double-headed arrow. One head pointing towards the “conduction box” and the other towards the “valence” box. The arrow is labeled, “Band gap.” The second diagram is similar to the first, but the band gap is about half as large. This diagram is labeled, “Semiconductor.” The third diagram is similar to the other two, but the band gap is about a fifth that of the “Semiconductor” diagram. This diagram is labeled, “Conductor.”

In order to conduct electricity, electrons must move from the filled valence band to the empty conduction band where they can move throughout the solid. The size of the band gap, or the energy difference between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band, determines how easy it is to move electrons between the bands. Only a small amount of energy is required in a conductor because the band gap is very small. This small energy difference is “easy” to overcome, so they are good conductors of electricity. In an insulator, the band gap is so “large” that very few electrons move into the conduction band; as a result, insulators are poor conductors of electricity. Semiconductors conduct electricity when “moderate” amounts of energy are provided to move electrons out of the valence band and into the conduction band. Semiconductors, such as silicon, are found in many electronics.
